blocks.text: “What do you mean, ask them questions?” I asked. I wanted to get him into a mood for talking.

“One way is to hit them over the head with a pole. Another way is to scratch their ears. Rich gentlemen sometimes want that when they want to show off a bit in front of their girls. I don’t mind the first one so much. I mean the hitting with a pole before I throw in their dinner. But I wait until they’ve had their sherry and coffee, so to speak, before I try the ear-scratching. Mind you,” he added, like a philosopher, “we have a lot of the same nature in us as those animals there. Here you come, asking me questions about my work. And I was so grumpy that I’d have seen you damned first before I answered, if it wasn’t for your blooming half-quid. I wouldn’t have answered even when you asked me, in a sarcastic way, if you should ask the Superintendent whether you could ask me questions. No offence, but did I tell you to go to hell?”

“And when you said you’d report me for using bad language, that was hitting me over the head. But the half-quid made that all right. I wasn’t going to fight, so I waited for my food. And I did my howling, the same as the wolves and lions and tigers do. But, Lord love your heart, now the old woman has pushed a piece of her tea-cake into me. She’s rinsed me out with her blooming old teapot, and I’ve lit up for a smoke. So now you can scratch my ears as much as you like. You won’t even get a growl out of me. Go on with your questions. I know what you’re coming to. It’s that escaped wolf.”

“Exactly. I want to hear what you think about it. Just tell me how it happened. When I know the facts, I’ll ask you what you think caused it. I’ll also ask you how you think the whole thing will end.”

“All right, boss. Here’s about the whole story. That wolf, the one we called Bersicker, was one of three grey wolves. They came from Norway to Jamrach’s, and we bought them from Jamrach four years ago. He was a nice, well-behaved wolf. He never gave any trouble worth talking about. I’m more surprised that he wanted to get out than I would be about any other animal in the place. But there, you can’t trust wolves any more than you can trust women.”
“Don’t mind him, sir!” Mrs. Tom broke in with a cheerful laugh. “He’s looked after the animals for so long that, bless me, he’s like an old wolf himself! But there’s no harm in him.”

“Well, sir, it was about two hours after feeding time yesterday when I first heard the trouble. I was making up a bed in the monkey-house for a young puma that is ill. But when I heard the yelping and howling, I came away at once. There was Bersicker, tearing at the bars like a mad thing, as if he wanted to get out. There weren’t many people around that day. Close by there was only one man. He was a tall, thin fellow with a hooked nose and a pointed beard, with a few white hairs running through it. He had a hard, cold look and red eyes. I took a kind of dislike to him, because it seemed as if he was the one the animals were angry at. He had white gloves of soft leather on his hands. He pointed out the animals to me and said: ‘Keeper, these wolves seem upset about something.’

“‘Maybe it’s you,’ I said, because I didn’t like the proud, important way he acted. He didn’t get angry, as I hoped he would. Instead he smiled a kind of rude, insolent smile. His mouth was full of white, sharp teeth. ‘Oh no, they wouldn’t like me,’ he said.
“‘Oh yes, they would,’ I said, copying the way he spoke. ‘They always like a bone or two to clean their teeth on around tea-time. And you’ve got a bagful.’

“Well, it was a strange thing. When the animals saw us talking, they lay down. And when I went over to Bersicker, he let me stroke his ears, the same as always. That man came over too. And bless me, he put in his hand and stroked the old wolf’s ears as well!”
